title: Manager Learning Circles
subject: Human Resources
description: How leaders and managers learn together in small peer groups: run a learning circle, build psychological safety, and turn what you learn into team practice.

lessons.title: What a learning circle is
lessons.body:
A learning circle is a small group of six to ten leaders who meet regularly to learn a topic together. Each meeting has a short input, a discussion, and a practice step the group applies at work before the next meeting.

Learning circles work because managers learn most from peers facing similar problems. The group becomes a place to test ideas, admit what is not working, and get honest feedback.

lessons.title: Running a session
lessons.body:
A simple 60-minute format:

1. **Check-in (5 minutes):** each person shares one thing from their last practice step.
2. **Input (15 minutes):** a short teaching piece, a case, or a guest speaker.
3. **Discussion (25 minutes):** structured questions, such as 'Where have you seen this?' and 'What would you do differently?'
4. **Commit (15 minutes):** each person chooses one practice step for the next two weeks, and says it aloud.

Rotate the facilitator, so no single person runs every session.

lessons.title: Psychological safety
lessons.body:
Learning requires admitting uncertainty. Psychological safety is the belief that you can speak up, ask questions, and make mistakes without being punished or humiliated. Research by Amy Edmondson at Harvard found it is a strong predictor of team learning.

Build it by:

- Asking questions yourself first, and admitting what you do not know.
- Thanking people who raise problems.
- Keeping what is said in the circle confidential, unless the group agrees otherwise.
- Not using learning-circle comments in performance decisions.

lessons.title: From learning to team practice
lessons.body:
Learning has no value until it changes how a team works. After each session, each manager should:

- Try one practice step with their team within two weeks.
- Ask the team what changed, and what did not.
- Report back at the next session with one example.

A practice step that is small and specific, such as 'hold a 10-minute coaching conversation on each deal this week', is more likely to stick than a general intention to improve.
